title: The additional prayer
hookLine: an extra Amidah on Shabbat and festivals, for the extra Temple offering

lines: JUST WHEN YOU THINK IT'S OVER.
cards: On a weekday, the morning service winds down after the Amidah to a few closing prayers and Aleinu. On Shabbat, after the long Torah reading, just when you think it's over, everyone stands up again.
Another silent Amidah, a whole extra prayer, at the end of a long morning. Visitors check how many pages are left. But this extra prayer is a mark of Shabbat and festival mornings.
To understand this extra prayer, you have to go back to the Temple, and count the animals.

teach.b: Musaf means added, or additional. In the Temple, every day had two fixed offerings, one in the morning and one in the afternoon. The daily prayers stand in their place.
But on Shabbat, the book of Numbers adds more: two more lambs, with flour and oil and wine, beyond the daily ones. Festivals and new moons got their own extra offerings too.
So when the Temple was gone and prayer took the place of sacrifice, the extra day got an extra prayer. A verse from Hosea is often quoted for this whole idea.
In the old Jewish translation: "So will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips." Words instead of animals. What's inside Musaf?
On Shabbat, the middle blessing names the day and recalls the extra offering from Numbers.
And here's where Jewish movements differ, openly. Orthodox prayer books keep the hope for the Temple's offerings to be restored.
Conservative prayer books keep Musaf but speak of the offerings as something our ancestors brought, in the past. Many Reform congregations leave Musaf out.
Each is a way of answering the same question: what do we do with the memory of sacrifice? And on Rosh Hashanah, Musaf grows three great sections, on kingship, remembrance and the shofar.
The kingship section opens with Aleinu, the prayer we met at the start of this stretch. Tradition says that was its first home.
An extra day gets an extra portion, of words.

how: Musaf is said after the Torah reading on Shabbat, festivals, Rosh Chodesh and the High Holy Days, as a silent Amidah with a repetition; Orthodox and Conservative congregations say it with different wording about the sacrifices, and many Reform congregations omit it.

o: the closing prayer said at the end of every service
the blessing said when the Torah is lifted up
the extra prayer added on Shabbat and festivals

s: every Jewish movement says Musaf in the same words
Orthodox, Conservative and Reform answer the sacrifices differently.
Musaf stands for the extra Temple offering on special days
Numbers adds two lambs on Shabbat beyond the daily offering.
tradition says Aleinu began in the Rosh Hashanah Musaf
it opens the kingship section there.

games.q: the Temple is gone, and Shabbat used to have an extra offering. what do the rabbis put in its place?
o: an extra Amidah: the offering of our lips.
games.why: an additional Amidah, Musaf, words in place of the extra offering, as Hosea's verse suggests.

practice: Look at what you were already going to do today, the ordinary offerings, so to speak: work, meals, the drive, the dishes.
Now picture adding one thing that wasn't required, a longer phone call, a walk, a slower meal, given just because the day deserves it.

wordCard.voice: Musaf. Additional. The extra Amidah of Shabbat, festivals and new moons, standing in for the extra Temple offering.

orig.note: Hebrew: added. the additional prayer of Shabbat and festivals.

carryVoice: Your line: an extra portion. Words now stand where the offerings once did. That's day six hundred twenty-one.
